CUTSA STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS AND CONTINUING MISAPPROPRIATION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Bayline Roofing Services, Inc.

PURPOSE OF THIS CUTSA STATUTE OF LIMITATIONS INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes the time limit for bringing a claim of trade secret misappropriation under the California Uniform Trade Secrets Act (Civ. Code, § 3426 et seq.) and its federal counterpart, the Defend Trade Secrets Act. It sets out the three-year limitations period and the discovery rule in Civil Code section 3426.6; the statutory rule that a continuing misappropriation constitutes a single claim; the California Supreme Court's explanation, in Cadence Design Systems, Inc. v. Avant! Corp., of when a misappropriation claim arises and why each later use or disclosure of the same trade secret by the same defendant augments the existing claim rather than starting a new one; the Court of Appeal's application of the discovery rule to the facts a trade secret owner knew or should have investigated (Glue-Fold, Inc. v. Slautterback Corp.; Cypress Semiconductor Corp. v. Superior Court); and the parallel three-year period in 18 U.S.C. § 1836(d). It is prepared by Jordan T. Reyes concerning the trade secret of Bayline Roofing Services, Inc., described as follows: The proprietary pricing model and supplier cost database used to prepare commercial roofing bids. The company first learned of facts suggesting misappropriation on or about January 15, 2026; the suspected misappropriation is believed to have begun on or about March 2024. This Information Sheet describes what the statutes and cited decisions say; it does not itself determine when any claim accrued, whether any claim is timely or time-barred, or whether any tolling rule applies in a specific dispute, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination.

THE THREE-YEAR LIMITATIONS PERIOD AND THE STATUTORY DISCOVERY RULE (CIVIL CODE § 3426.6)
The California Uniform Trade Secrets Act contains its own statute of limitations. An action for misappropriation must be brought within three years after the misappropriation is discovered or, by the exercise of reasonable diligence, should have been discovered. The three-year period therefore does not necessarily begin on the date the misappropriation occurred; the statute builds a discovery rule into the limitations provision itself, so that the period is measured from actual discovery or from the point at which reasonable diligence would have led to discovery, whichever comes first. The same section adds a second sentence, addressed in a separate clause, providing that for purposes of the limitations period a continuing misappropriation constitutes a single claim.

A CONTINUING MISAPPROPRIATION IS A SINGLE CLAIM (CIVIL CODE § 3426.6, SECOND SENTENCE)
The second sentence of Civil Code section 3426.6 provides that, for purposes of the limitations section, a continuing misappropriation constitutes a single claim. Read together with the definition of misappropriation in section 3426.1, subdivision (b) -- which reaches acquisition by improper means as well as disclosure or use of a trade secret without consent -- the sentence addresses the situation in which a defendant who has once misappropriated a trade secret goes on using or disclosing it over time. The statute treats that ongoing course of conduct as one claim rather than as a series of separately accruing claims, which means the three-year period is not restarted by each later use. What this sentence means for when the single claim arises, and for what happens if the initial misappropriation was discovered more than three years before suit, was the subject of the California Supreme Court's decision in Cadence Design Systems, Inc. v. Avant! Corp., described in the following clauses.

THE CALIFORNIA SUPREME COURT'S HOLDING: A MISAPPROPRIATION CLAIM AGAINST A GIVEN DEFENDANT ARISES ONLY ONCE (CADENCE DESIGN SYSTEMS V. AVANT!)
In Cadence Design Systems, Inc. v. Avant! Corp., the California Supreme Court answered a question certified to it by the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit: under the California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, does a claim for trade secret misappropriation arise only once, when the initial misappropriation occurs, or anew with each subsequent misuse of the trade secret? The case arose from a 1994 settlement in which Cadence had released all claims it then had against Avant!; Cadence later discovered evidence that Avant!'s software had been built from copied Cadence source code and sued in December 1995, and the parties disputed whether the release covered Avant!'s continued use of the source code after the release date. The Supreme Court held that a plaintiff's claim for misappropriation of a trade secret against a defendant arises only once, when the trade secret is initially misappropriated, and that each subsequent use or disclosure of the secret augments that initial claim rather than giving rise to a separate claim. The court described its answer as narrow: it did not decide how the parties to the particular release had intended to define the term "claim," only that the statute views a continuing misappropriation of one party's trade secret by another as a single claim.

"MISAPPROPRIATION" HAPPENS WITH EACH MISUSE, BUT THE "CLAIM" ARISES ONCE (CADENCE)
The Cadence court drew a distinction between a misappropriation and a claim. Reading the statutory definition of misappropriation -- which covers wrongful acquisition as well as each disclosure or use of a trade secret without consent -- together with the single-claim sentence of Civil Code section 3426.6, the court explained that a misappropriation occurs not only at the time of the initial wrongful acquisition but also with each later misuse or wrongful disclosure, while a claim for misappropriation arises for a given plaintiff against a given defendant only once, at the time of the initial misappropriation, subject to the discovery rule in section 3426.6. Each new misuse or wrongful disclosure is viewed as augmenting that single claim of continuing misappropriation rather than as giving rise to a separate one. The court also explained what the undefined statutory term "continuing misappropriation" means: the continuing use or disclosure of a trade secret after it was acquired by improper means or as otherwise specified in section 3426.1, subdivision (b). In the court's account, the drafters of the uniform act thereby affirmed the Ninth Circuit's earlier decision in Monolith Portland Midwest Co. v. Kaiser Aluminum & Chemical Corp., which had applied California common law, and rejected the contrary view that misappropriation gives rise to multiple claims each time the secret is misused or disclosed. The court rejected both parties' positions in their strongest forms: it did not accept Avant!'s view that only the initial breach of confidence is a misappropriation, and it did not accept Cadence's view that each new use is a new claim.

THE UNIFORM ACT'S OFFICIAL COMMENT: NO "CONTINUING WRONG," BUT A DELAYED START (GLUE-FOLD)
In Glue-Fold, Inc. v. Slautterback Corp., the Court of Appeal explained the origin of Civil Code section 3426.6 and gave substantial weight to the drafters' official comment. The court noted that section 3426.6 is derived almost verbatim from section 6 of the Uniform Trade Secrets Act as originally drafted, and that when a statute is adopted from a uniform act without change it is appropriate to accord substantial weight to the commissioners' comment on it. The comment the court quoted acknowledges that, before the uniform act, courts were divided on whether trade secret misappropriation is a continuing wrong -- the Ninth Circuit's Monolith decision holding that under California law it is not, so that the limitation period for all recovery begins with the initial misappropriation, and the D.C. Circuit's Underwater Storage decision treating each act of misappropriation as starting its own period. The comment then states that the act rejects a continuing wrong approach to the statute of limitations but delays the commencement of the limitation period until an aggrieved person discovers or reasonably should have discovered the existence of misappropriation, and that if objectively reasonable notice of misappropriation exists, three years is sufficient time to vindicate one's legal rights. The section therefore trades a rolling limitations period for a later starting point.

THE FIRST DISCOVERED (OR DISCOVERABLE) MISAPPROPRIATION STARTS THE THREE YEARS (GLUE-FOLD; CYPRESS SEMICONDUCTOR)
The Court of Appeal in Glue-Fold surveyed the federal decisions construing section 3426.6 and found them unanimous that it is the first discovered, or discoverable, misappropriation of a trade secret that commences the limitation period. The court tied this to the statutory definition of misappropriation, which reaches acquisition, disclosure, or use of a trade secret: any one of those methods of betraying a confidence may be the misappropriation whose actual or constructive discovery starts the clock, and the limitation period is not triggered solely by what the statute calls a continuing misappropriation. Eight years later, in Cypress Semiconductor Corp. v. Superior Court, a different panel of the same court summarized the effect of the single-claim sentence in the same terms: the first discovered or discoverable misappropriation commences the limitation period. Under these decisions, whether the first act was an improper acquisition, a disclosure, or a use does not matter for limitations purposes; what matters is when the trade secret owner discovered, or with reasonable diligence should have discovered, that first act.

A PAUSE IN THE MISAPPROPRIATOR'S CONDUCT DOES NOT RESTART THE PERIOD (GLUE-FOLD)
Glue-Fold illustrates how the single-claim rule operates when a misappropriator stops and later resumes. Glue-Fold had disclosed a new glue-application process to Slautterback under a nondisclosure agreement; Slautterback then sold and advertised a product incorporating the process. Glue-Fold alleged that it discovered the misappropriation in August 1995 and protested in October 1995; Slautterback discontinued its public advertising until June 1996 and then resumed it; Glue-Fold sued in January 1999. Glue-Fold argued that the interruption made the post-1996 activity a second, separate period of misappropriation with its own three-year period. The Court of Appeal rejected that theory. It held that the actual discovery of an act of misappropriating a trade secret commences the three-year period, which is not tolled by the misappropriator's subsequent inactivity, and that the period is likewise not tolled if that inactivity is followed by what the uniform act calls a continuing misappropriation. What occurred after the initial discovery was, in the court's words, not a separate claim but an integral part of what section 3426.6 deems a single claim; allowing the plaintiff to focus only on the later activity would contravene the rule against splitting a cause of action and would condone the continuing wrong approach the drafters repudiated. Because Glue-Fold's suit was filed more than three years after its admitted discovery, the trade secret claim was time-barred and summary judgment was affirmed.

ONCE A DEFENDANT IS KNOWN TO HAVE MISUSED ONE SECRET, IT IS UNREASONABLE TO ASSUME IT WILL PROTECT OTHERS (GLUE-FOLD, QUOTING INTERMEDICS)
The Glue-Fold court acknowledged that trade secret misappropriation is ordinarily covert and hard for the betrayed party to discover, a point recognized both before and after the uniform act's adoption. It nonetheless adopted, as its own view of California law, a federal district court's statement in Intermedics, Inc. v. Ventritex, Inc. that California law assumes that once a plaintiff knows or should know that a particular defendant cannot be trusted with one secret, it is unreasonable for that plaintiff simply to assume that the defendant can be trusted to protect other secrets. In a footnote the court set out the fuller passage from Intermedics, which reasons that by rejecting the continuing wrong theory while insisting on discovery as the trigger, the Legislature focused on the plaintiff's interest in real notice that the defendant's conduct had jeopardized all the confidences shared with that defendant, and that such a law imposes on plaintiffs a responsibility to take prompt and assertive corrective action with respect to all of their interests whenever they detect a fracture in a once confidential relationship. On the facts, the court observed that Glue-Fold had its first clue about Slautterback's unreliability when Slautterback asked for permission to market the product in the fall of 1992, and that this, together with the August 1995 discovery of an earlier sale, constituted actual notice of the misappropriation.

"DISCOVERY" MEANS THE PLAINTIFF'S REASON TO SUSPECT WRONGDOING, NOT PROOF OF A WINNING CLAIM (CYPRESS SEMICONDUCTOR)
In Cypress Semiconductor Corp. v. Superior Court, the Court of Appeal addressed what discovery means under section 3426.6. Silvaco Data Systems had sued a former employee's new company for incorporating Silvaco's source code into a product; that company's customers, including Cypress, had licensed the product. After obtaining a judgment against the company in 2003, Silvaco notified the customers and sued Cypress in 2004. The trial court ruled that the claim against Cypress could not have accrued until Cypress itself learned, in August 2003, that the product contained Silvaco's trade secrets, because a defendant's knowledge is an element of misappropriation. The Court of Appeal disagreed. Applying the California Supreme Court's general discovery-rule decisions in Norgart v. Upjohn Co. and Fox v. Ethicon Endo-Surgery, Inc., it held that it is not the law that accrual depends on the existence, as a matter of fact, of a winning claim; a plaintiff has reason to discover a cause of action when it has reason at least to suspect a factual basis for its elements, understood as the generic elements of wrongdoing, causation, and harm. The discovery referred to in section 3426.6 is the plaintiff's discovery, and the proper focus is not on the defendant's actual state of mind but on the plaintiff's suspicions. A plaintiff's later inability to prove the defendant's mental state means it cannot prevail on the merits, but does not retroactively affect the running of the statute. The court concluded that the statute began to run when Silvaco had any reason to suspect that the customers knew, or should have known, that they had acquired Silvaco's trade secrets -- a question the court held could not be answered as a matter of law on the record before it, and which it left for a jury.

SEPARATE DEFENDANTS CAN MEAN SEPARATE CLAIMS WITH SEPARATE PERIODS (CYPRESS SEMICONDUCTOR; CADENCE)

SECTION 3426.6 IMPOSES NO DUTY TO NOTIFY THIRD PARTIES, BUT DELAY CAN FEED OTHER DEFENSES (CYPRESS SEMICONDUCTOR)

THE SINGLE-CLAIM CONCEPT REACHES RELEASES, AND DOES NOT SHRINK THE REMEDIES FOR LATER USES (CADENCE)
Cadence argued that because section 3426.6 says a continuing misappropriation is a single claim only "for the purposes of this section," the concept should be confined to the statute of limitations and should not affect what a settlement release covers. It reasoned that if a continuing misappropriation is a single claim for limitations purposes, it is difficult to see how it could be more than one claim for purposes of litigation generally: a plaintiff could not legitimately plead separate claims for each misuse of a trade secret without impermissibly evading the statute of limitations, and there was no indication the Legislature intended "claim" to mean one thing in litigation and another in releases. The court also answered Cadence's concern that treating continuing misappropriation as one claim would give a misappropriator a de facto license once a release was signed. It observed that parties to a release in a trade secret dispute remain free to fashion the release as broadly or narrowly as they choose, and that a successful trade secret plaintiff is entitled to the full panoply of remedies -- injunctive relief against further misappropriation under section 3426.2, damages for actual loss under section 3426.3, and relief from unjust enrichment -- so that the potential damages encompassed by a single continuing-misappropriation claim may expand with each illicit use or disclosure. In short, the single-claim rule affects when the claim arises and how many claims there are; it does not cap what the one claim can recover.

Reading the statutory definition of misappropriation -- which covers wrongful acquisition as well as each disclosure or use of a trade secret without consent -- together with the single-claim sentence of Civil Code section 3426.6, the court explained that a misappropriation occurs not only at the time of the initial wrongful acquisition but also with each later misuse or wrongful disclosure, while a claim for misappropriation arises for a given plaintiff against a given defendant only once, at the time of the initial misappropriation, subject to the discovery rule in section 3426.6. Glue-Fold had disclosed a new glue-application process to Slautterback under a nondisclosure agreement; Slautterback then sold and advertised a product incorporating the process. What occurred after the initial discovery was, in the court's words, not a separate claim but an integral part of what section 3426.6 deems a single claim; allowing the plaintiff to focus only on the later activity would contravene the rule against splitting a cause of action and would condone the continuing wrong approach the drafters repudiated. Because Glue-Fold's suit was filed more than three years after its admitted discovery, the trade secret claim was time-barred and summary judgment was affirmed.

expectedJSON.body: In Cypress Semiconductor Corp. v. Superior Court, the Court of Appeal addressed what discovery means under section 3426.6. Silvaco Data Systems had sued a former employee's new company for incorporating Silvaco's source code into a product; that company's customers, including Cypress, had licensed the product. After obtaining a judgment against the company in 2003, Silvaco notified the customers and sued Cypress in 2004. The trial court ruled that the claim against Cypress could not have accrued until Cypress itself learned, in August 2003, that the product contained Silvaco's trade secrets, because a defendant's knowledge is an element of misappropriation. The Court of Appeal disagreed. Applying the California Supreme Court's general discovery-rule decisions in Norgart v. Upjohn Co. and Fox v. Ethicon Endo-Surgery, Inc., it held that it is not the law that accrual depends on the existence, as a matter of fact, of a winning claim; a plaintiff has reason to discover a cause of action when it has reason at least to suspect a factual basis for its elements, understood as the generic elements of wrongdoing, causation, and harm. The discovery referred to in section 3426.6 is the plaintiff's discovery, and the proper focus is not on the defendant's actual state of mind but on the plaintiff's suspicions. A plaintiff's later inability to prove the defendant's mental state means it cannot prevail on the merits, but does not retroactively affect the running of the statute. The court concluded that the statute began to run when Silvaco had any reason to suspect that the customers knew, or should have known, that they had acquired Silvaco's trade secrets -- a question the court held could not be answered as a matter of law on the record before it, and which it left for a jury.

Kadisha, in which officers, directors, and investors who joined a corporation after its initial misappropriation were held potentially liable for later use; the court read Kadisha as holding only that there may be separate claims of continuing misappropriation among different defendants, with differing dates of accrual and types of tortious conduct -- some defendants liable for the initial misappropriation, others only for later continuing use. The Court of Appeal rejected that reading to the extent Forcier so held, reasoning that under it a plaintiff could lose its claim against a third party before that party ever came in contact with the trade secret, and that malevolent third parties would merely have to lie low and wait out the clock. The court held that a plaintiff may have more than one claim for misappropriation, each with its own statute of limitations, when more than one defendant is involved -- which is different from saying that each misappropriation gives rise to a separate claim, the result section 3426.6 precludes. A cause of action against a third-party defendant accrues with the plaintiff's discovery of that defendant's misappropriation, and any continuing misappropriation by that defendant constitutes a single claim.

The Court of Appeal found no such duty in section 3426.6. It reasoned that the misappropriation that triggers the statute is the one the plaintiff suspects, not one that may or may not actually exist; where the owner knows a third party holds its secret but also knows the third party has no reason to know of the owner's claim, there has been no actual misappropriation and nothing to suspect, and the plain language of the statute imposes no duty to notify in that situation. The court added, however, that the statute's substantive provisions supply their own incentives for prompt notice: a trade secret loses protection if the owner does not undertake reasonable efforts to keep it secret, and good-faith acquirers who do not receive notice before materially changing position may not be liable for misappropriation at all. The Supreme Court rejected the argument. It reasoned that if a continuing misappropriation is a single claim for limitations purposes, it is difficult to see how it could be more than one claim for purposes of litigation generally: a plaintiff could not legitimately plead separate claims for each misuse of a trade secret without impermissibly evading the statute of limitations, and there was no indication the Legislature intended "claim" to mean one thing in litigation and another in releases. The court also answered Cadence's concern that treating continuing misappropriation as one claim would give a misappropriator a de facto license once a release was signed. It observed that parties to a release in a trade secret dispute remain free to fashion the release as broadly or narrowly as they choose, and that a successful trade secret plaintiff is entitled to the full panoply of remedies -- injunctive relief against further misappropriation under section 3426.2, damages for actual loss under section 3426.3, and relief from unjust enrichment -- so that the potential damages encompassed by a single continuing-misappropriation claim may expand with each illicit use or disclosure. In short, the single-claim rule affects when the claim arises and how many claims there are; it does not cap what the one claim can recover.
